# A Map of Places to Sit

The first bench my father put on the map was not a bench. It was a low wall outside the dentist’s office, built to contain three hydrangeas and failing, by late July, to contain any of them. He backed into the flowers, sat, and started his stopwatch.

“What are we timing?” I asked.

“How long before somebody comes out and tells me I can’t sit here.”

Nobody came out. Across the road a man carried a sheet cake sideways out of the supermarket, discovered what he had done, and went back in. My father watched with the grave interest he generally reserved for people trying to reverse a trailer.

“Two minutes,” he said.

“Is that enough?”

“For what?”

I had no answer. He put a blue dot on the map.

The map was a free handout from the council offices. On one side were the streets of Bellwether, with little pictures of the clock tower and the war memorial. On the other side was an advertisement for a housing development that had been cancelled after somebody found a protected newt. My father had taken six copies. The council woman had asked whether he was expecting visitors. He had said he hoped not.

He was seventy-four and had recently begun having trouble walking. This was not how he described it. He said his legs were getting less interested in the second half of a journey. Home to the bakery was no problem. Bakery to home was sometimes a matter of stopping outside the betting shop and pretending to read the racing results until he could make it to the corner.

The council had removed the benches from the high street in March. The notice said they were being taken away for refurbishment. By June, someone had unscrewed the little brass plaques from their backs and put them in a drawer at the council offices. My father knew this because he had gone in to ask when the benches were coming back and had been offered, instead, a plaque. He could choose whichever one he liked.

“I didn’t know any of the dead people,” he told me. “It seemed forward.”

I was staying with him for two weeks while the bathroom in my flat was being redone. I had brought a laptop, three novels, and the belief that I would be useful. In the first four days I reorganized his kitchen cupboards, arranged for a grocery delivery he did not want, and suggested that he move his bedroom downstairs.

“Downstairs where?”

“The dining room.”

“Where would I have dinner?”

“You could have dinner in the kitchen.”

He thought about this for a moment. “Where would I have breakfast?”

I got angry, although he had scarcely moved. Later I put the mugs back on their original shelf. He had kept them beside the kettle, which was where I would have put them if I’d been trying to make the kitchen easier to use rather than trying to make it look as though I had done something.

The map was his idea. He wanted to find a way to the bakery that did not depend on a sudden interest in horses. I volunteered to go along. I had work to do, but my father liked to leave the house at eleven, and at eleven I generally began looking at property listings in places where I had no intention of living. I could spare the time.

We developed a key. A blue dot meant somewhere you could sit without buying anything. A green dot meant you probably ought to buy something. A circle around either meant there was a backrest. The bus shelter got a blue dot with a question mark because the seat consisted of a narrow metal ledge pitched at an angle. My father tried it and found that it required most of the muscles he was hoping to rest.

“Good place to get your trousers wet,” he said. “We should have a symbol for that.”

By our third outing he had begun to ask people. The florist told us you could sit on the concrete step beside her shop as long as it wasn’t Thursday, when the flowers came. A woman posting a letter directed us to the cemetery, where there were three benches and a fourth if you counted the lid of a water tank. A boy in school uniform told us that if we went into the carpet shop and acted like we were waiting for our mum, the man would let us sit on the stairs.

“How old do you have to be?” my father asked him.

The boy considered it. “Probably younger than you.”

We eventually found a route to the bakery by way of the dentist’s wall and the church porch. It added six minutes and avoided the betting shop. My father bought four buns to celebrate. He ate one standing outside the bakery, which I thought was an eccentric way to mark the occasion, but the icing was coming off on the paper and he didn’t want to waste it.

On the way back we found a woman sitting on the dentist’s wall. She had a red shopping trolley and a packet of frozen peas balanced on her knee. My father kept walking. At the corner he stopped and examined the map.

“You could have sat beside her,” I said.

“There wasn’t room.”

“There was loads of room.”

“For the two of us, yes. Not for the two of us and her wanting to be on her own.”

He said this without looking up. I went back to the supermarket and bought a bottle of water we didn’t need, to give him a reason to stay where he was. When I came out, he had been joined by the woman with the frozen peas. They were talking about the price of washing powder. Before she went on, she asked whether he was all right. He said he was waiting for me. That seemed to satisfy them both.

On Friday I took the map to the copy shop.

I meant to make two copies, one for him and one to leave at the bakery. The woman behind the counter asked what it was, and when I told her, she said her mother had stopped coming into town after the benches went. She had assumed it was because the bank had closed. Her mother had a habit of doing three errands at once and objected to anything that brought the number down to two.

The woman made twenty copies and charged me for two.

By Monday there were none left at the bakery. Someone had photographed one and put it on the Bellwether community page, where people immediately began arguing about whether we were encouraging loitering or failing to encourage it in enough parts of town. The florist rang to ask if we could make the bit about Thursdays bigger. The churchwarden rang to say there was no need to make anything bigger, but that a man had eaten a whole rotisserie chicken in the porch and left the bag.

“Was he sitting down?” my father asked.

There was a silence. I could hear the clock in the hall.

“Yes,” the churchwarden said.

“Well,” my father said, and then, apparently thinking better of whatever he had meant to say, promised to go down and get the bag.

On Tuesday the dentist came out.

We were not sitting on his wall at the time. We were across the road, waiting for a gap in the traffic. He waved the map at us. My father waved back. A van went by, and when it was quiet again the dentist said, “Could I have a word?”

He was younger than I’d expected, and he had the exhausted courtesy of someone who had already spent the morning asking people to open a little wider. A patient had tripped over somebody’s shopping trolley on Monday. It had been on the pavement in front of the wall. The patient hadn’t been hurt, he said, but she could have been.

I started to explain that the map was unofficial. In the middle of the explanation I heard myself making the argument that because nobody had asked us to do something, nobody could ask us to stop.

My father said, “We’ll take you off.”

The dentist folded the map twice, lining up the edges carefully. “My dad used to sit there,” he said. “When he came to pick me up. He’d get here half an hour early. Drove me mad.”

He looked back at the wall. In the heat the hydrangeas had gone limp over the pavement.

“I don’t mind people sitting,” he said. “I mind not knowing what I’m supposed to do when there’s a problem.”

My father asked if his dad was still driving. The dentist said yes, unfortunately, and for a little while the two of them talked about the roundabout by the bypass. Then we all went our separate ways.

At home I drew an X through the blue dot. My father watched me do it.

“You don’t have to press that hard,” he said.

I had made a hole in the paper. I taped it from the back, over the newt development.

That evening he brought out one of the other copies. Almost all the places we had marked clustered around the high street. In the streets to the east, where there were rows of council houses and a long incline to the health centre, we hadn’t put anything at all.

“I never go up there,” he said.

“You don’t have to.”

“No. But other people do.”

We set out the next morning. Halfway up the hill there was a bus stop with no shelter and a sign advertising a service that ran on Tuesdays and Fridays. It was Wednesday. A woman in slippers stood at the gate of the nearest house, shaking crumbs off a tea towel. My father asked her if there was anywhere to sit.

“Here, if you want,” she said.

She went inside and came back with two folding chairs. One had a picture of a tropical fish on the seat. She set them up inside her gate and told us to mind the step. My father sat on the fish.

The woman’s name was Jean. She had worked at the health centre until it moved to the top of the hill. Her husband, who was inside watching the snooker, used to bring a chair out for a particular man who walked to his appointments. The man always wore a tie. He had diabetes and a small dog and had been dead six years. Jean knew his appointments used to be on Wednesdays because Wednesday was when her husband went out to bring in the bins, and one day he had left the chair open on the pavement and the bin lorry had backed over it. They’d bought the fish chair after that.

“Can we put you on our map?” I asked.

“No,” she said. “I don’t want people knocking.”

“Fair enough,” my father said.

“But you can finish sitting.”

We did. Somewhere inside the house the snooker audience applauded. Jean folded her tea towel into thirds over the gate and told us about a woman who had tried to get a bench installed at the bus stop. The council had sent a form asking the woman to estimate how many people would use it. She had written back that the people in a position to find out were the ones who could stand there all afternoon.

“Did they write back?” I asked.

“Probably. She liked a letter. I think half the pleasure was getting one back.”

On the way down the hill I walked ahead and then had to wait. My father came slowly after me, touching the tops of walls where he could. It occurred to me that he had known on the way up exactly what the way down would cost him. I had been thinking of the hill as somewhere we were going to look.

At the bottom, he asked me to hold his elbow. I did, and immediately began steering him toward a front step.

“Just hold it,” he said.

We stood there until he was ready.

In the second week the council put one of the old benches back. It was outside the bakery, which had complained about people leaning on the window. There was a fresh coat of varnish and a pale oblong on the back where the plaque had been. My father took a cloth in his pocket, in case the varnish was still tacky. It wasn’t. He sat and moved his hands along the grain of the seat. Then he got up again because a woman with two carrier bags was coming and he thought she might be put off if he looked settled. She walked straight past him into the bakery. He sat back down.

We made a new edition of the map. The bench got its blue dot and its circle. The dentist’s wall disappeared. We added a note about the florist’s deliveries and a dotted line up the hill, where there was still nowhere to sit unless Jean happened to be shaking out her tea towel. We did not put that on the map.

My father said he’d take twenty copies to the council offices. I asked what he wanted them to do with the maps.

“Look at them.”

“And then?”

He slid the copies into a supermarket bag so the edges wouldn’t curl. “Well, I’ll be there. They can ask.”

I didn’t go with him. The plumber had called to say he’d finished my bathroom and left the key with the upstairs neighbour, who was going away the next morning. I packed my laptop and the three novels, two of them unread. Before I left I wrote my father a list of the food in the fridge, then threw it away. He had bought most of it himself.

At the station my train was delayed. There were two benches on the platform, both occupied, and I watched a woman walk past them to the far end, turn, and walk back. She was carrying a bunch of flowers wrapped in brown paper. The paper crackled each time she changed hands. I had spent two weeks watching people do things that might or might not mean they needed to sit down. I still couldn’t always tell.

A man on the bench next to me stood when the train was announced. I put my bag between my feet and moved over, though there was enough room already. The woman came and sat. She kept the flowers upright on her lap, holding them by the paper with both hands. We waited. The announcement had been for a train on the other platform.

After a while she turned to me. “Gladioli,” she said.

I had been trying to think what they were called. My mother used to buy them when they were cheap, which they often were, because they were inconvenient to get home. She used a tall glass vase that leaned to one side unless you put something under it. My father used to fold a corner of the newspaper and slide it under the base. Then at breakfast he’d ask who had taken the sports section.

I could have told the woman some of this. There was time. Instead I said they were a good colour. They were pale green, a colour I hadn’t known gladioli came in. She tipped the bundle a little so I could see the buds all the way up.

“Those ones at the top won’t open,” she said. “Not unless I cut the bottom ones off when they go. I always forget.”

When my train arrived, she stayed where she was. I’d assumed she was getting on it too. Through the window I saw her set the flowers down on the bit of bench I’d left, then reach over to tuck the loose paper underneath them. Before the train pulled away, a man came out of the station carrying two cups. She took the flowers straight back onto her lap. He sat down beside her, close enough that she could take the lid off his cup while he held it.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A literary short story built around a daughter and her father making a map of places to sit in their town.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and gently funny, with humor that never makes the father’s reduced mobility or the town’s indifference into a joke. Its pathos comes through small adjustments: the father’s legs becoming “less interested” in a journey, the daughter discovering that reorganizing his kitchen was more about her wish to help than his needs, and the care in how he makes room for strangers’ privacy. The story invites the reader to notice the conditions that make ordinary public life possible—and to question the assumption that needing a place to rest is a private inconvenience rather than a shared concern.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story centers benches, walls, bus stops, maps, and the minor negotiations of sitting down without buying anything. It foregrounds dignity and agency in aging, practical kindness, and the limits of well-intentioned help. The closing image of the flowers being shifted to make room for a companion echoes the larger theme: making space can be an unshowy act, and recognizing what someone needs is not always the same as deciding for them.

## Evidence line
> I had spent two weeks watching people do things that might or might not mean they needed to sit down.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The recurring map-and-seating motif, restrained humor, and careful attention to agency give this sample a distinctive and coherent moral perspective.
